title: 1.6.2 Group PA Part 2: Build It
description: Turn the chart you just passed into a documented, straight-line program. Ten checks, all of them things Chapter 1 taught. Auto-graded: submit up to three times and your best counts. After your third try you can see how it is solved, once your teacher releases it.

steps.title: Fill in the header
steps.instructions: The top of script.js has three comment lines waiting: Problem, Partners, Date. Fill all three in. Both partners' names, on the Partners line, before anything else happens.

steps.title: Copy your pseudocode in as comments
steps.instructions: Your plan from 1.6.1, written out one instruction per line as // comments, indented to show what sits inside the decision. Do this before you write a single line of JavaScript. If a line does not say what you meant in the plan, fix the wording now.

steps.title: Declare the inputs
steps.instructions: One variable per number your problem takes in, plus one string for the name or label. Descriptive camelCase names -- pricePerPizza, not p. The limit you are comparing against never changes, so declare it with const.
hints: The limit is the fixed number in your problem statement: 2.00, 15.00, 70, or the trip distance
const goodDealLimit = 2.00; -- const is what says it never moves, and the name stays camelCase like every other name
A name someone else can read is worth more marks here than a short one

steps.title: Work out the value
steps.instructions: One line of arithmetic that turns your inputs into the one number your problem is about: the cost per slice, the cost per person, the weighted average, the range of a tank. Name it for what it is.

steps.title: Answer the diamond without an if
steps.instructions: Your plan's yes-or-no question is a comparison, and a comparison produces a boolean (1.2.18). Store it: const meetsTheLimit = yourValue <= yourLimit; That variable IS the question. Underneath it, write the two branches as pseudocode comments, one starting IF and one starting ELSE, both in capital letters -- what the program would say on the yes answer, and on the no side. Chapter 2 turns those comments into an if statement; today they stay comments.
hints: Which way round the comparison goes depends on your problem -- read your chart, not the example
The two branch comments are graded. IF and ELSE, in capitals, one comment line each

steps.title: Report it
steps.instructions: At least three console.log calls, and at least one of them a template literal with a ${} in it so the numbers are inside the sentence rather than bolted onto the end. Also print typeof for one of your values -- an assessment of Chapter 1 that never asks what type anything is has skipped 1.2.

steps.title: Read it back to each other
steps.instructions: Swap the keyboard. The partner who did not type reads the program out loud line by line while the other checks it against the chart. Every shape on the chart should appear once, in order. Fix what does not match, then run three sets of numbers through it -- you will need them for the demo writeup.

requirements.title: Both partners named in the header
requirements.description: The Partners line at the top of script.js has names on it. Help: 1.2.2 (Declaring Variables with let and const)
requirements.hint: Line 3 of script.js: // Partners: -- put both names after the colon.

requirements.title: The problem is named in the header
requirements.description: The Problem line says which of the four menu problems this is. Help: 1.6.1 (Group PA Part 1: Design the Plan)
requirements.hint: Line 2 of script.js: // Problem: -- Slice Economics, Split the Check, Grade Forecast or Fuel Stop.

requirements.title: The limit is a const
requirements.description: The number that never changes is declared with const, not let. Help: 1.2.2 (Declaring Variables with let and const)
requirements.hint: const goodDealLimit = 2.00; -- const rather than let, because it never changes. The name is camelCase like every other name.

requirements.title: A string variable is declared
requirements.description: One variable holds text -- the name or label your problem talks about. Help: 1.2.2 (Declaring Variables with let and const)
requirements.hint: Something like const pizzeriaName = "Tony's"; -- quotes make it a string.

requirements.title: A number variable is declared
requirements.description: At least one variable holds a number typed straight in. Help: 1.2.2 (Declaring Variables with let and const)
requirements.hint: let sliceCount = 8; -- no quotes around a number, or it is a string.

requirements.title: The value is computed from the inputs
requirements.description: A variable is assigned from arithmetic on other variables, not typed in by hand. Help: 1.2.2 (Declaring Variables with let and const)
requirements.hint: const costPerSlice = pizzaPrice / sliceCount; -- the answer has to be worked out, not written down.

requirements.title: The diamond is stored as a boolean
requirements.description: A comparison is assigned to a variable, which is what the plan's question becomes. Help: 1.2.2 (Declaring Variables with let and const)
requirements.hint: const meetsTheLimit = costPerSlice <= goodDealLimit; -- a comparison produces true or false (1.2.18).

requirements.title: Both branches written as pseudocode
requirements.description: An IF comment line and an ELSE comment line, sitting below the stored comparison, say what happens on each answer to the question. Help: 1.6.1 (Group PA Part 1: Design the Plan)
requirements.hint: Two comment lines, capitals, BELOW the line that stores the comparison: // IF meetsTheLimit THEN report it is a good deal   and   // ELSE report it is not. The pseudocode you copied in at the top does not count on its own.

requirements.title: A template literal reports the result
requirements.description: At least one console.log uses backticks with ${} inside. Help: 1.2.2 (Declaring Variables with let and const)
requirements.hint: console.log(`A slice costs $${costPerSlice}.`); -- backticks, not quotes, and ${} around the variable.

requirements.title: typeof is reported for one value
requirements.description: The program prints the type of at least one of its values. Help: 1.2.23 (The typeof Operator)
requirements.hint: console.log(typeof costPerSlice); -- 1.2.23. Say what type your computed value actually is.

aiCheck.rubricTitle: What the AI read in your code
aiCheck.prompt: The student wrote JavaScript for the group performance-assessment part "1.6.2 Group PA Part 2: Build It". The task they were given: Turn the flowchart you passed in Part 1 into a documented, straight-line program: a header naming both partners and the problem, a const limit, a string and a number variable, a value computed from the inputs, the chart's decision stored as a boolean, both branches written as IF and ELSE comment lines, a template-literal report and a typeof report. You cannot run their code: read it and judge what it WOULD do in a browser. The header is in comments at the top of script.js, so for the header criteria read the comments. Judge each criterion by whether the idea is achieved, however the student wrote it. Different variable and function names, template strings, arrow functions, semicolons, spacing, quotes and order are all fine. Do not require any particular structure unless the criterion names one. Mark a criterion missing only when the idea is absent or the code does the opposite. Code inside a comment never runs. Write each note for THIS student's own code: in a not-met note, name the exact line or name in their code that causes the problem (quote at most a few words of it), say in plain words what it does now versus what the criterion needs, and give one concrete next thing to try, but do NOT write the corrected code. In a met note, say in one short phrase what in their code satisfied it. Do not use generic praise.
